# MIDI Play BASIC Extension Reference

> This is an English translation of the [Japanese original](../basic-reference.md). Where the two differ, the Japanese version is authoritative.

The specification of the statements that MIDI Play BASIC Extension adds to BASIC, and of the Music Macro Language (MML) that can be used in the `PLAY` statement.

Migration from the original MSX-MIDI BASIC extension is covered separately in [`diff-from-msxmidi.md`](diff-from-msxmidi.md).

## What it does

Once a MIDI interface is set up with `CALL MIDI`, the playback of the `PLAY` statement goes out to MIDI.

- The MIDI channels that can sound at the same time are **1-16**
- Rhythm MML can be used in **only one string**, and its default destination is **channel 10**
- It cannot play together with the PSG or the FM sound chip
- It does not receive MIDI

---

## Statements

### CALL MIDI

```
CALL MIDI [(<mode> [, <interface number>])]
```

Prepares for MIDI playback. **Until this statement is executed, `PLAY` does not go out to MIDI, and `CALL STOPM` cannot be used.**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| Mode | `0`, `1`, `4` or `5` (write the sum of the values in the table below) / `-1` = release. `0` when omitted |
| Interface number | `0` or omitted: auto-detect (when run again, the one currently in use is kept). The numbers are in "[Interface numbers](#interface-numbers)" |

The mode packs two independent settings into one number; write it as their sum.

| Value | Description |
|---|---|
| `0` | Without rhythm. The playback tick is 1/60 second |
| `1` | With rhythm (the **first string** of `PLAY` becomes rhythm MML) |
| `4` | Generates the playback tick from the **high-precision timer** ("[The playback tick](#the-playback-tick)") |

`2`, `3`, `6` and `7` cannot be used (`Illegal function call`). Specifying `4` for an interface that has no high-precision timer also gives `Illegal function call`, and **in that case nothing changes** — the interface already in use and the tick both stay as they are.

**The memory available to BASIC decreases by 1912 bytes, and all variables are cleared**. Playback uses interrupts, so system throughput drops accordingly.

At initialization, it sends All Sound Off (CC#120) and Reset All Controllers (CC#121) to all 16 MIDI channels. It does not send voices or channel roles ("[Sound module settings](#sound-module-settings)").

When the interface is omitted or `0` is written, it is auto-detected. **If none is found, the result is `Illegal function call`** — nothing can be started until the device to play is determined. In this case the memory does not decrease and the variables are not cleared.

```basic
CALL MIDI                :' without rhythm, interface auto-detected
CALL MIDI(1)             ' with rhythm
CALL MIDI(4)             ' generate the tick from the high-precision timer
CALL MIDI(5)             ' with rhythm + high-precision timer
CALL MIDI(0, 8)          ' name MIDI Saurus (port A) explicitly
CALL MIDI(-1)            ' release
```

Writing a comment with `'` directly after `CALL MIDI` with its arguments omitted gives `Syntax error`. Separate it with `:`, as in `CALL MIDI :'…`. The same applies to `CALL STOPM`.

**`CALL MIDI` can be run again after it has already been executed**. This is used to switch the mode, and to return the channel assignment of `@H`, the velocity, the rhythm note numbers and the tempo to their default values. Writing an interface number switches to that interface; omitting it or writing `0` keeps the one currently in use. The memory does not decrease any further, and the variables are not cleared. If a sequencer was running with `@S1` or `@S2`, it sends Stop (`FCh`) before switching.

#### CALL MIDI(-1)

Returns the allocated memory and interrupts, and goes back to the state before `CALL MIDI` was executed. Playback stops, and **all variables are cleared.**

If a sequencer was running with `@S1` or `@S2`, it also sends Stop (`FCh`) at this time. The clock source itself goes away, so this keeps the receiver from being left running. It is not sent after stopping with `@S0`.

Calling it when `CALL MIDI` has not been executed gives `Illegal function call`.

#### Interface numbers

| Number | Interface | Auto-detection |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | Leave it to auto-detection (same as when omitted) | ― |
| `1` | MSX-MIDI (built into the FS-A1GT, MIDI Interface 3, external μPACK) | ○ |
| `2` | Philips NMS1205 | ○ |
| `3` | YAMAHA SFG-01 / SFG-05 | ○ |
| `4`-`7` | (reserved) | ― |
| `8` | BIT2 MIDI Saurus (port A) | × |
| `9` | BIT2 MIDI Saurus (port B) | ×, not supported |
| `10` | MSX MIDI Interface (homebuilt, i8251) | × |
| `11` | MSX MIDI Interface 2 (homebuilt, channel A) | × |
| `12` | MSX MIDI Interface 2 (homebuilt, channel B) | × |
| `13` | Tada MIDI (printer port) | × |
| `14` | JOY MIDI (joystick port 1) | × |
| `15` | JOY MIDI (joystick port 2) | × |

Specifying a number skips the auto-detection search.

- When **an interface that can be auto-detected (`1`-`3`)** is specified, the result is `Illegal function call` if it is not actually found
- **An interface that cannot be auto-detected (`8` and above)** is accepted as is, because the MSX has no means of checking whether it is present
- Specifying a reserved number (`4`-`7`) or an unsupported one (`9`) gives `Illegal function call`

An interface with two MIDI OUT outputs has a separate number for each output.

### CALL BGM

```
CALL BGM(<0/1>)
```

Specifies whether `PLAY` plays in the background. With `0`, `PLAY` does not return until playback ends; with `1`, it returns immediately.

Initialization by `CALL MIDI` sets background playback, so **this setting returns to `1` each time `CALL MIDI` is executed.**

Values other than `0` / `1` give `Illegal function call`. Calling it when `CALL MIDI` has not been executed also gives `Illegal function call`.

### CALL MDR

```
CALL MDR(<B>, <S>, <M>, <C>, <H>)
```

Sets the note numbers that `B` `S` `M` `C` `H` play in rhythm MML. It rewrites the same place as `%<letter>=n;` in MML, so whichever is executed later remains.

| Argument | Contents |
|---|---|
| `<B>`-`<H>` | The note number that the letter plays (0-127). **None of the five can be omitted** |

**The order of the arguments is `B` `S` `M` `C` `H`**, unrelated to the order in which the letters are written in MML. Passing `0` makes that letter silent.

```basic
CALL MIDI(1)
CALL MDR(35, 40, 41, 51, 44)
PLAY "BSMCH4"
```

The remaining five letters (`A` `D` `E` `F` `G`) cannot be assigned with this statement. Use `%<letter>=n;` in MML.

The assignment returns to the GM drum kit each time `CALL MIDI` is executed. Calling it when `CALL MIDI` has not been executed gives `Illegal function call`.

### CALL STOPM

```
CALL STOPM
```

Stops a `PLAY` that is playing in the background. It empties the queue, returns the parts to their defaults, and sends note-off for the sounding notes. The MIDI channels set with `@H` and the velocities set with `@K`, `Vn` and `@K<letter>=n;` are kept. The rhythm accent (`@An`) is a part setting, so it returns to the default of 127.

Calling it when `CALL MIDI` has not been executed gives `Illegal function call`.

### PLAY

```
PLAY [#<sound chip number>,] <string 1> [, <string 2> ... [, <string 16>]]
```

Plays according to the MML written in `<string>`. Unlike the other extended statements, it needs no `CALL`.

**Up to 16 strings.** There are 16 MIDI channels, and one string plays one channel. Channels that are not used can simply be left out. With rhythm, the first string is for rhythm, so there are 15 for melody.

**Up to 10 strings built by expressions per `PLAY` statement.** Listing 11 or more strings built by concatenation or functions, such as `"O4C4"+A$` or `MID$(A$,3)`, gives `String formula too complex`. String constants (`"CDE"`) and string variables (`A$`) are not counted toward this however many are listed, so to use more than that, put the strings into variables first.

```basic
PLAY "O4C4"+A$, "O4E4"+A$                 ' two strings built by expressions. OK
B$="O4C4"+A$
PLAY B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$,B$     ' with a variable, even 11 is OK
```

`<sound chip number>` is `0`-`3`, and **all have the same meaning** (MIDI). Omitting it is the same. `4` or more gives `Illegal function call`. It is accepted so that programs written with `PLAY#2,` for MSX-MUSIC can be brought over as they are.

There is no argument that specifies the correspondence between `PLAY` strings and MIDI channels. With `@H` in MML, any channel can be specified for each string. If none is specified, 1, 2, 3, … are assigned in order from the first string. **Only when rhythm is used does the melody assignment skip 10** — 10 belongs to the first string (rhythm). Without rhythm, 10 is also assigned normally.

```basic
CALL MIDI
PLAY "O4CDE", "O3GAB"          ' 1st string → CH1, 2nd string → CH2

CALL MIDI(1)
PLAY "BSH8H8", "@H1O4CDE"      ' 1st string → rhythm (CH10), 2nd string → CH1
```

### Statements of the MSX Sound Suite cartridge build

**In the MSX Sound Suite cartridge build (the build in the Y8960 cartridge), the following four become statements that switch to another sound BASIC extension on the same cartridge.**

```basic
CALL MUSIC     ' switches to MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2
CALL AUDIO     ' switches to MSX-AUDIO BASIC Extension Lite
CALL MINIT     ' switches to Y8960 BASIC Extension
CALL OPM       ' switches to OPM BASIC Extension
```

Switching returns what this BASIC extension reserved, and playback stops. The arguments are read by the destination BASIC extension, so their form follows that extension.

In the standalone cartridge build, these four are not registered. If another cartridge with the same names is inserted, it handles them; otherwise they give `Syntax error`.

### Statements that are not provided

For the following, this BASIC extension **does not register the names at all**. If another cartridge with the same names is inserted, it handles them as usual; otherwise they give `Syntax error`.

| Category | Statements |
|---|---|
| Voice | `CALL VOICE` `CALL VOICE COPY` |
| Temperament and pitch | `CALL PITCH` `CALL TEMPER` `CALL TRANSPOSE` |
| Sound chip registers | `CALL AUDREG` |
| Getting the playback state | `CALL PLAY` |

Because MIDI approaches these differently, select voices with `@n` and bend pitch with `P` in MML. Send sound-module settings such as temperament with `@C`, `@N`, `@R` and `Zn`, following the sound module's manual.

## Music Macro Language

The basic grammar, such as notes, rests, lengths, octaves and tempo, is the same as the MML of MSX-MUSIC BASIC Extension V2.

### Writing numbers

Numbers in MML are written in decimal. With `$`, they can be written in hexadecimal. **`$` is always followed by exactly two digits**, in the range `$00`-`$FF`. `A`-`F` may be upper or lower case. For a negative value, write `-` first (`P-$64`).

```basic
PLAY "O$04C4"        ' O4, then C as a quarter note
PLAY "@C$07,$40"     ' the same as @C7,64
```

The number of digits is fixed because **`A`-`F` are both hexadecimal digits and note names**. If digits were read until they ran out, note names placed after the number would also be taken into it. Because counting stops after two digits, nothing written after them is added to the number. Inserting a space does not change this (spaces are skipped).

**Ending with one digit is `Illegal function call`.** If `$F` were allowed, it could not be told apart from `$FC` when a `C` follows, so write `$0F` with two digits. A third digit is not added to the number and is read as the next command.

```basic
PLAY "O$4"           ' → Illegal function call. Write O$04
PLAY "V$0FF"         ' V15, then plays the note F
```

**Values whose absolute value is 256 or more cannot be written in hexadecimal.** For `Pn` and `@Pn` (-1200 to 1200), and for the `r` of `@Nr,d` and `@Rr,d` (0-16383), write values whose absolute value is above 255 in decimal.

**Write a length of `0` in decimal.** `C$00` and `R$00` do not become a note or rest that consumes no time; they are treated the same as writing them with the length omitted.

Writing `=x;` instead of a number uses the value of the BASIC variable `x`.

### MML list

| Character | Meaning | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A`-`G` | Plays a note. `0` can be given as the length | | |
| `+` `#` | Raises the note by a semitone | | |
| `-` | Lowers the note by a semitone | | |
| `.` | Multiplies the length of a note or rest by 1.5 | | |
| `Ln` | Sets the length | 1-96 | `L4` |
| `Rn` | Rest. `0` can be given | 0-96 | `R4` (inside a tuplet, the tuplet length) |
| `On` | Sets the octave | 1-8 | `O4` |
| `>` | Raises the octave by one | | |
| `<` | Lowers the octave by one | | |
| `Nn` | Plays the note at the pitch given by n | 0-96 | |
| `Qn` | Ratio of the sounding length | 1-8 | `Q8` |
| `Tn` | Sets the tempo | 32-255 | `T120` |
| `{ }n` | Tuplet. A rest also counts as one note. "n × number of notes" must also be 96 or less | 1-96 | The value of `Ln` |
| `&` | Joins the notes before and after it (tie / legato) | | |
| `~n` | Moves smoothly to the next note (portamento) | 0-127, can be omitted | |
| `@Wn` | Waits for the length of an nth note while the sound keeps playing | 1-96 | The value of `Ln` (even inside a tuplet) |
| `=x;` | Sets the number from variable x | | |
| `Xx;` | Plays the MML stored in string variable x (*1) | | |
| `@n` | Selects a voice (program change) | 0-127 | |
| `@m,l,p` | Selects a voice with the bank specified | 0-127 | |
| `@Hn` | The MIDI channel this string plays on | 1-16 | In string order |
| `<note name>[<length>],n` | Sets the velocity of that note only | 0-127 | The value of `@K` |
| `@Kn` | The value used when the velocity is omitted | 0-127 | 100 |
| `Vn` | Specifies the same thing as `n*8` | 0-15 | |
| `@Vn` | Volume (CC#7) | 0-127 | |
| `@En` | Expression (CC#11) | 0-127 | |
| `@In` | Panning (CC#10). `0` is left, `64` is the center, `127` is right | 0-127 | |
| `@Mn` | Modulation (CC#1) | 0-127 | |
| `Pn` | Pitch bend (cents, absolute) | -1200 to 1200 | `P0` |
| `@Pn` | Pitch bend (cents, added to the current value) | -1200 to 1200 | |
| `@Cr,d` | Control change r = d | 0-127 | |
| `@Nr,d` `@Nm,l,d` | NRPN | Below | |
| `@Rr,d` `@Rm,l,d` | RPN | Below | |
| `Zn` | Sends one byte of MIDI data as is | 0-255 | |
| `@Sn` | Signal to a sequencer | 0-2 | |

- (*1) No macro can be written after this macro. Writing one causes an error

The note name `O4C` corresponds to MIDI note number 60 (middle C). The range is from `O1C` (24) to `O8B` (119). In `Nn`, 0 corresponds to 24, the same as `O1C`, 36 corresponds to 60, the same as `O4C`, and 96 becomes 120 (a semitone above `O8B`).

**Write the tempo (`T`) at the head of the first string.** A `T` written there takes effect on all strings. What `T` determines is the speed of the notes read in after it. `PLAY` reads the strings from the start a little at a time in turn, so if `T` is changed in the middle of a piece, the change starts from that point in that string, but where it starts in the other strings depends on how far they had been read by then, and does not line up with the position where it is written. Writing a separate `T` in each string does not give each string its own tempo.

**Lengths go up to 96.** `L96`, `C96` and the rest `R96` can be written. However, whether fine lengths can actually be timed depends on the interface ("[Differences between interfaces](#differences-between-interfaces)").

**Inside a tuplet (`{ }n`), a rest also counts as one note and also takes the tuplet's length.** `{CDR}1` is a tuplet of three notes, and `R` is a third rest, the same as `C` and `D`. As with notes, a written length takes precedence: the `R` in `{CDR12}1` is a twelfth rest. `@Wn` is not counted as a note, and even when its length is omitted it waits for the length of `Ln`, not the tuplet length. `L8{C@WD}2` has the length of two quarter notes and one eighth note.

### Voices and channels

`@n` sends a program change. `@m,l,p` sends bank select (CC#0 = m, CC#32 = l) and then sends program change `p`.

`@Hn` sets the MIDI channel this string plays on. If it is not written, channels are assigned in the order of the `PLAY` strings. It can also be written in the string for rhythm.

### Velocity

Velocity can be written for each note with `<note name>[<length>],n`. The value used when it is omitted is set with `@Kn` (0-127, default 100). `Vn` is a way of specifying the same thing as `n*8`; `V15` is 120. Writing just `V` with the argument omitted is the same as `V8`.

```basic
PLAY "@K80 O4CDE C4,120"       ' the first 3 notes are 80, only the last C is 120
```

`@Vn` (CC#7) and `@En` (CC#11) move the volume on the sound source side and are separate from velocity.

### Pitch bend

`Pn` shifts the pitch in cents. `@Pn` adds to the current bend value. Both have the range -1200 to 1200.

The width of the bend is determined by a setting on the sound source side (the bend range). The default is 2 semitones, and when the bend range is changed with `@R0,n`, the bend follows it. If a cent value beyond the range is written, it bends only as far as the range allows.

### Ties and portamento

`&` joins the notes before and after it. It sends legato on (CC#68 = 127) at the start of the joined span and legato off (CC#68 = 0) at its end.

`~` sends, in addition to the same legato as `&`, portamento on (CC#65 = 127) / off (CC#65 = 0). Writing `~n` sends portamento control (CC#84) with `n` as the note number to glide from.

In GM2, `&` and `~` are guaranteed to work only in mono mode. Send `@C126,1` (mono mode ON) before using them.

**If playback stops in the middle of `&` or `~`, the legato / portamento setting remains in the sound source**. With any of an error, CTRL-STOP or `CALL STOPM`, the sounding notes stop but the setting stays as it is, so the first note of the next `PLAY` may sound joined. Running `CALL MIDI` sends Reset All Controllers and restores it.

### Length 0 and waiting

Giving `0` as the length of a note **issues only a note-on and consumes no time.** `R0`, conversely, **issues only a note-off and consumes no time.** `@Wn` waits for the length of an nth note while the sound keeps playing.

Combining these lets you move the pitch and volume within a single note.

```basic
PLAY "T120O4C0@W8P100@W8P200@W8R0"
```

`C0` issues the note-on; then, waiting an eighth note at a time, the pitch is raised to 100 and then 200 cents, and finally `R0` issues the note-off. The total length is three eighth notes.

**Constraint — a second note cannot be placed without advancing time**. After a note of length 0, if nothing that advances time (`@Wn`, or an `Rn` with a length) is placed before the next note, it is `Illegal function call`.

```basic
PLAY "C0D0"      ' → Illegal function call
PLAY "C0R0D0"    ' → Illegal function call (R0 does not advance time)
PLAY "C0@W8D0"   ' → OK
```

`L0` and `@W0` are `Illegal function call`. Write length 0 explicitly on each note, as in `C0`.

### Sending raw MIDI data

| Command | Content |
|---|---|
| `@Cr,d` (0-127) | Control change r = d |
| `@Nr,d` | Data d to NRPN r. `r` (0-16383) is sent split into MSB / LSB |
| `@Nm,l,d` | Data d to NRPN MSB = m, LSB = l |
| `@Rr,d` | Data d to RPN r |
| `@Rm,l,d` | Data d to RPN MSB = m, LSB = l |
| `Zn` (0-255) | Sends one byte of MIDI data as is |

NRPN sends the number with CC#99 / CC#98 and RPN with CC#101 / CC#100, and for the data only Data Entry MSB (CC#6) is sent. Data Entry LSB (CC#38) is not sent.

### Signals to a sequencer

| Command | Content |
|---|---|
| `@S0` | Stop (`FCh`) |
| `@S1` | Start (`FAh`) |
| `@S2` | Continue (`FBh`) |

`@Sn` is a message without a channel, so it is delivered regardless of the channel specified with `@H`. The same messages can also be sent from rhythm MML.

After `@S1` or `@S2`, **MIDI clock (`F8h`) keeping time with the tempo is sent continuously** (24 times per quarter note). Changing `T` also changes the clock speed, and `@S0` stops it. The clock does not stop when `PLAY` ends.

However, the clock is sent only **when timing with the high-precision timer** — when `4` is added to the `CALL MIDI` mode — and otherwise only the status byte of the signal is sent. The speed after starting is then left to the receiver ("[The playback tick](#the-playback-tick)").

After starting with `@S1` or `@S2`, executing `CALL MIDI(-1)` or running `CALL MIDI` again **sends Stop automatically**. This is because both stop the clock. After stopping with `@S0`, it is not sent.

### Rhythm MML

With `CALL MIDI(1)`, the first string of `PLAY` is for rhythm. List the letters of the percussion to play, then write the length after them.

```
<letter>[!][<letter>[!]...]<length>
```

| Example | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `B4` | Plays `B` for the length of a quarter note |
| `BS4` | Plays `B` and `S` at the same time |
| `BS!4` | Plays `B` normally and `S` with an accent, at the same time |

A length of `0` cannot be written. `B0`, `B$00` and `B=X;` (with `X` equal to 0) all give `Illegal function call`.

| Command | Description | Range | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%<letter>=n;` | Assigns the note number that `<letter>` sounds | 0-127 | Below |
| `@K<letter>=n;` | Velocity of `<letter>` | 0-127 | 100 |
| `@An` | Velocity when `!` is attached | 0-127 | 127 |

`<letter>` is one of 10 letters: `A`-`H`, `S` and `M`. The following five are assigned from the start (the GM drum kit), and the other letters do not sound until they are assigned. Writing `%<letter>=0;` makes that letter stop sounding.

| Letter | `B` | `S` | `M` | `C` | `H` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Note number | 36 | 38 | 45 | 49 | 42 |

These five letters can also be assigned together with [`CALL MDR`](#call-mdr). Both rewrite the same place, so whichever is executed later is what remains.

When letters sound at the same time, the letters with an accent are sent first, and within each group the order is `A`→`H`→`S`→`M`.

Drums send only note-on. This is because GM specifies that note-off is ignored on the rhythm channel, and drums decay naturally.

**Only the following have meaning in rhythm MML.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Percussion | `A`-`H` `S` `M` `!`, and the length and `.` after them |
| Rhythm only | `%<letter>=n;` `@K<letter>=n;` `@An` |
| Shared with melody | `Rn` `Tn` `@Hn` `@n` `@m,l,p` `@Vn` `@En` `@In` `@Mn` `@Cr,d` `@Nr,d` `@Rr,d` `@Pn` `@Wn` `@Sn` `=x;` `Xx;` |

There is no `Ln`, so write the length after every list of percussion. If the length of `@Wn` is omitted, it waits for a quarter note. `On` `Qn` `{ }n` `&` `~` `Pn` `Zn` are not available either, and writing them gives `Illegal function call`.

`Vn` and `@Kn` do not give an error when written, but they have no effect, because the velocity of percussion is decided by `@K<letter>=n;` and `@An`.

```basic
CALL MIDI(1)
PLAY "BSH8H8S!H8H8"
```

- Plays the bass, snare and hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the snare with an accent together with the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note
- Plays the hi-hat, and waits for an eighth note

### Commands that cannot be used

`Sn` (envelope shape), `Mn` (envelope period) and `Yr,d` (register write to the sound chip) have no counterpart in MIDI, so they cannot be used. Writing them gives `Illegal function call`.

`S` and `M` in rhythm MML are percussion letters, and are separate from these.

---

## Differences between interfaces

### The playback tick

The playback tick is chosen from two. Adding `4` to the mode of `CALL MIDI` selects the **high-precision timer**; otherwise it is **1/60 second**, and **the default is 1/60 second**. On PAL (the European video standard) machines, everything written as 1/60 second becomes 1/50 second.

| | 1/60 second (default) | High-precision timer (`4` added to the mode) |
|---|---|---|
| Tick | Fixed at 1/60 second | Linked to the tempo. One of 48, 96 or 192 ticks per quarter note is chosen according to the tempo |
| 96th note | When `T` exceeds 150, they **sometimes cannot be written in a row** (below) | **Sounds at any tempo** |
| MIDI clock (`@S`) | Not sent | Sent |
| BASIC speed | 60 interrupts per second | 100-204 per second. **BASIC slows down accordingly** (below) |

**Being able to write lengths up to 96 is the same with either**; what differs is whether they can be timed. The ratios of note lengths and the way `T` works do not change with either.

#### Lengths too short for 1/60-second ticks

With 1/60-second ticks, **a note whose tempo × length exceeds 14400 cannot have a length**. This is `L96` at `T151` and above, and `L64` at `T226` and above; on PAL (the European video standard) the figure is 12000, so it is `L96` at `T126` and above, and `L64` at `T188` and above.

In that case:

- **A single such note sounds**. The remainder is carried over to the next note
- **Writing a note right after a note that could not have a length gives `Illegal function call`.** `PLAY` stops there. If the string is short, not a single note sounds; if it is long, it sounds partway and then stops
- Which note cannot have a length depends on how the remainder has accumulated so far. If a remainder has accumulated before, a run of short notes may get through. If the run goes on long enough, it always stops somewhere
- Playback can continue if **something that advances time** — a rest with a length (`R`) or `@Wn` — is placed in between

```basic
PLAY "T255L96C"        ' sounds
PLAY "T255L96CD"       ' Illegal function call
PLAY "T255C96R48D96"   ' sounds (the rest advances time)
```

**This does not happen in rhythm MML or with `@Wn`.** Anything shorter than a tick carries the remainder over to the next, and percussion that falls into the same tick sounds together. Percussion has no note-off, so nothing is lost by sounding together.

It does not happen with the high-precision timer. The tick is linked to the tempo, so a 96th note has at least 1 tick at any tempo.

The high-precision timer can be used with **the three that `CALL MIDI` can auto-detect** — MSX-MIDI (number `1`), Philips NMS1205 (`2`) and YAMAHA SFG-01 / SFG-05 (`3`). With the other interfaces, which are used by specifying their number (`8` and above), adding `4` to the mode gives `Illegal function call`.

**On machines where MSX-MIDI interrupts do not arrive, it falls back to 1/60 second**. Adding `4` to the mode does not give `Illegal function call`, and playback works as is — everything in the table above is as in the "1/60 second" column.

#### How much the high-precision timer slows BASIC down

**It varies greatly with the number of parts sounding**. Below is the time taken to run the same BASIC loop, shown as the increase over the time before `CALL MIDI` is executed. With an SFG-05 connected to an MSX2+ (Z80):

| What is sounding | 1/60 second | High-precision timer |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing sounding | +2% | +45% |
| 1 part | +9% | +80% |
| 8 parts | +21% | +161% |
| 16 parts | +25% | **+405%** |

**Playing 16 parts with the high-precision timer on an MSX2+ brings BASIC down to about 1/5 of its speed**. Playback also cannot keep up. Measured with an SFG-05, a piece becomes about 15% longer, and the ratios of note lengths break down. It does not stop. To play many parts on an SFG with an MSX2+, use 1/60-second ticks or reduce the number of parts.

**With the MSX-MIDI built into the turbo R, the same 16 parts stay within +25%**. It also varies with the interface; even on an MSX2+, the Philips NMS1205 is lighter than the SFG (+212% with 16 parts).

#### Tempo accuracy

**With either tick, a single part stays within 1% of the time the tempo represents**. The direction and size of the deviation differ.

With many parts, there is a separate delay. MIDI takes 0.32 milliseconds to send 1 byte, so when 16 parts change notes all at once, the note-offs and note-ons take 96 bytes, about 31 milliseconds of sending. With 1/60-second ticks, the ticks that passed during that time are made up afterwards, so even with 16 parts on an MSX2+ and an SFG-05, the length of a piece changes by less than 2%. With the high-precision timer, they cannot all be made up; the same 16 parts make the piece about 15% longer, and the shorter the note, the more the ratios of lengths break down.

| Tick | Deviation |
|---|---|
| 1/60 second | About +0.13% at any tempo (the TV's video period itself) |
| High-precision timer, SFG-01 / SFG-05 | -0.1% to -0.5% (depending on the tempo, always on the short side) |
| High-precision timer, Philips NMS1205 | -0.9% to +0.6% (depending on the tempo) |
| High-precision timer, MSX-MIDI | Almost 0 (±0.02%) |

To match a long piece with a recording or other equipment, **the high-precision timer of MSX-MIDI is the most accurate**, followed by 1/60 second. The size of the deviation varies with the tempo on the SFG and the NMS1205, which use the sound chip's timer, because the period of 1 tick has a fraction that differs for each tempo. The SFG always deviates on the short side, while the NMS1205 runs fast or slow depending on the tempo.

**At the finest level, only the SFG cannot keep up with sending**. With the high-precision timer, a run of 96th notes at `T240` (96 notes per second) makes playback about 10% longer on the SFG-01 and SFG-05. **When it is inserted in an expanded slot, the delay is larger still**. All notes sound, and the ratios of lengths between notes do not change. This does not happen on MSX-MIDI or the NMS1205. Up to 48th notes at `T240`, up to 96th notes at `T120` — keeping to 48 notes per second avoids it on the SFG as well (the same in an expanded slot).

### Other restrictions

- **Only `&H00`-`&HF7` can be sent to the MIDI Saurus.** `&HF8` and above (system real-time messages) are used by the interface itself, so they are not sent. This applies to `@Sn` and the MIDI clock, the Stop that `CALL MIDI` sends automatically, and `&HF8` or above written in `Zn`
- **Tada MIDI and JOY MIDI do not run at the correct speed on machines with an HD64180**. This is because the transmit timing is generated from the Z80's execution time
- **When an SFG (SFG-01 / SFG-05) is inserted, that module's own `CALL MUSIC` cannot be used**. At startup, this ROM removes the SFG's BIOS from handling `CALL` — otherwise the SFG-01 breaks other `CALL`s, including `CALL MIDI`. This does not affect using the SFG as a MIDI interface

---

## Sound module settings

`CALL MIDI` sends no settings to the sound module. Send the following from MML as needed. The procedure differs between sound sources, so see the manual of the sound source.

| What to do | What to send (for GM2) |
|---|---|
| Make a channel the rhythm part | `@C0,120` + program change |
| Make `&` / `~` take effect | `@C126,1` (mono mode ON) |
| Select a voice | `@n` / `@m,l,p` |
| Change the bend range | `@R0,n` |

Selecting with rhythm changes only how `PLAY` reads its MML; the role of the channel on the sound source side does not change.
